The Best Bed Frames, Tested in Our Own Rooms (2026)

📅 06 May 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, to find the best bed frames, the WIRED Reviews team has put more than 35 to the test over the years.
  • Recent findings suggest that be sure to check out our other sleep guides, including the Best Mattresses, Best Hybrid Mattresses, Best Japanese Joinery Bed Frames, Best Bedsheets, and Best Sleep Gifts for more.
  • According to recent reports, updated November 2026: We've added new bed frames from Castlery and Quince.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, to find the best bed frames, the WIRED Reviews team has put more than 35 to the test over the years. Our top pick is Thuma's Classic Bed, but we've also got options for different budgets and preferences. A good bed frame can improve the look of your room, but it also contributes to sleep hygiene and extends the life of your mattress. I've rounded up the team's favorites below, with prices reflecting queen-size frames where applicable.

Recent findings suggest that be sure to check out our other sleep guides, including the Best Mattresses, Best Hybrid Mattresses, Best Japanese Joinery Bed Frames, Best Bedsheets, and Best Sleep Gifts for more. And if you don't want to upgrade your frame just yet, check out this advice on how to fix bed frame problems.

According to recent reports, updated November 2026: We've added new bed frames from Castlery and Quince. We've also checked for accuracy throughout.

I've owned the Thuma Classic Bed for five years, and it feels as good as upcoming. You don't need a single tool to assemble this solid wood bed frame. The company uses traditional Japanese joinery techniques, and it took me about 15 minutes to put the whole thing together. That means disassembly and reassembly when I had to move was so easy—there are just two thumb screws at the top and bottom edges of the frame, which you can tighten by hand once everything else is in place.

Industry observers note that more surprising is how sturdy it is. I've gone through so many bed frames before the Thuma, and after a year or two, there's usually a broken slat or bent metal rod here and there. Or the slats keep falling down, so you have to do that thing where you pull the mattress over your head as you try to shove them back in place (just me?). The Thuma doesn't creak and never slides around. The foam Pillowboard is an additional expense, but it's comfy. Thuma has since added a wood headboard, which is pricier, but that's what I'll probably upgrade to next, since it completes the look. The only downside is how expensive this whole bed frame is (the price has jumped since I first purchased it), but if it helps, the Thuma is made from repurposed wood, and it's UL GreenGuard Gold Certified, meaning low chemical emissions. —Julian Chokkattu.

Thuma made its name with a minimalist wooden bed (our top pick, above) with clean lines and a tool-free assembly process that's no more complex than snapping together Lego bricks. The Signature was debuted in February 2025 as the brand's first fully upholstered bed. The Thuma Signature has the same Japanese wood joinery at its heart for easy assembly, but covers the frame in soft Italian felted wool or performance linen for a decidedly more posh experience. I've been testing the wool version for a few months. It took less than five minutes for me to assemble, and it's very solid and dead silent, with no squeaking whatsoever. The plush headboard upholstery is pillow-soft, and my only problem with it is remembering not to just lay my head directly on it. Best of all, when it's time to move, this bed pops apart in just a few minutes without any bolts or screws. —Martin Cizmar.

DreamCloud (queen, with bamboo headboard).

I really admire Japanese joinery bed frames, not just because of their minimalistic beauty but also their easy, tool-free setup. Trust me, we don’t want my clumsiness around sharp objects. Not all bed frames that follow this blueprint are of the same caliber, with some being far more stable than others, and the price point usually reflects that. DreamCloud's bamboo Japanese joinery bed frame wasn’t just gorgeous, but outfitted with small details that make a substantial impact. These include tiny additional rods on each of the boards, located where they are stacked atop each other at the ends. The idea is to keep each of the rails that make up the frame even more secure than just the tension of the overall design. There are included foam blocks if you decide to throw in a headboard, so there's no banging against the wall, either. Plus, I’ll never argue with the price tag, which is very within my budget. —Julia Forbes.

According to recent reports, I was broker than broke when I got my first apartment more than a decade ago, and this cheap bed frame I bought from Amazon is still being circulated among my younger family members. It's as simple as simple gets, but the steel construction means the frame is durable, and you don't need to add a box spring. The 18-inch model leaves a cavernous space beneath the bed that can accommodate several tote-style storage containers—which could be a blessing or a curse depending on the usual state of your bedroom floor. Just keep in mind that there is no edge whatsoever. This thing is basically a table for your mattress, but it'll get the job done.

Recent findings suggest that I've tested nearly a dozen different bed frames during my time leading this coverage area for the WIRED Reviews team, and the Saatva Siena is probably the prettiest and most elegant I've ever tried. The leather upholstery just makes it feel so grown-up. It's sexy but not straight out of a dark romance dungeon. It's a statement piece that blends in with my decor. I like the free in-room delivery and the rich smell of leather. However, while the frame itself is exceedingly stable, it does slide around on my hardwood floors (I'm planning on attaching some rubbery grips to the feet to remedy this). My main complaint is that you can see the slats of the frame when you're close to the mattress. From a distance, it looks OK, but the white slats are so obvious up close, if you're looking, that it takes away from the whole put-together effect for me. It's also the perfect awkward height to attract dust bunnies that can be difficult to clean unless you move the bed to sweep or vacuum. Overall, these drawbacks are minor, and I still think this frame is worth your consideration. I'll just cross my fingers that none of my Hinge dates look too closely.

When the crib phase ends, this is the bed to get. I upgraded my son from a crib that converted into a toddler bed into this actual kids’ bed, and everyone is sleeping better for it. Nestig originally caught my eye for its adjustable crib, and the Nestig Wave Kids Bed shares similar design elements, with its wooden headboard and side panels. This bed frame can be used as either a Montessori-style floor bed or a standard twin, depending on whether you add the legs. It can accommodate a variety of twin-sized mattresses, and my son loves climbing into his bed each night and demanding I lie down with him while we read. The floor bed aspect is handy since I quietly roll out of the bed and onto the floor to escape his grip, and I like knowing that if my son rolled out of bed, he doesn’t have far to go. When it's time to add the legs, I'll have to take the frame apart partially, which is a small con but not a deal-breaker. —Nena Farrell.

Small bedroom? Mobility challenges? Don’t want to block a window? You might want to consider a low-profile frame. They’re typically under 11 inches high as opposed to around 20 inches for a traditional frame, which means you may not get as much under-bed storage, but for many, the benefits outweigh this drawback. (The Cooper has about 7 inches of clearance off the floor.) I personally have been grappling with not wanting to block a large window with a headboard, and I was curious if a low-profile frame might be the answer. Sure enough, it was—this 38-inch-tall frame hits just 2 inches below the windowsill and looks fantastic. In fact, the minimalist, mid-century-inspired Cooper is practically indistinguishable from similar frames being sold by Pottery Barn and Crate and Barrel, but runs around $500 less.

With its angled legs and rounded corners, the Cooper definitely has Thuma vibes, but does not feature Japanese joinery construction. It requires some assembly; namely, joining the rails together and screwing down the slats. If you’d rather not deal with this, white-glove delivery is available for $199. For my test unit, it took the delivery driver about 20 minutes to assemble, and in the few months I’ve had it, there haven’t been any squeaks, creaks, or loosening hardware. Note that an 8- to 12-inch mattress is recommended. —Kat Merck.

If you prefer the look of fabric covers, the Awara Platform frame will be a good fit. It's simple to assemble, and the pieces are easy to move. The spruce wooden slats are all attached together, so once you have the four frame pieces assembled, simply roll the slats out and they'll attach via hook-and-loop closures to the frame itself. The frame's height is nice, too. It's elevated just enough to make your bed look refined, but not so much that you'll end up losing things underneath your mattress. Though be aware, I did seem to stub my toes on this bed frame more than others I've tested.

According to recent reports, this adjustable base is from the makers of one of our favorite mattresses overall and one of our favorite mattresses for side sleepers. It runs on electricity to move the hydraulic-like motors below, which raise both the head and foot area of the bed. It comes with a wireless Bluetooth-enabled remote with buttons to adjust the head and foot portion of the bed up and down, a built-in flashlight, and a button to bring the frame down to a flat level.

Industry observers note that the Legget & Platt app can act as a remote as well—a huge sigh of relief for a generally scatterbrained person like myself who's prone to losing things. In the app, you name your bed, make the adjustments, and save your favorite positions so you can easily go back to them. The bed frame is sleek—not bulky at all—and is around 13 inches off the ground, making extra storage space underneath that I didn’t have before. The legs are virtually invisible, although the zero-clearance design allows the base to be used without the legs if using platform bases.

Recent findings suggest that the adjustable frame rises in half-inch increments from 13 to 18 inches from the original base, and the motor is fairly quiet. The base works with mattresses designed to flex, without shifting inside materials or weakening the structure, and is compatible with nearly all Saatva mattresses. For non-Saatva mattresses, check with the manufacturer to ensure it's compatible with an adjustable base.

Sources indicate that saatva provides a 10-year warranty as well as free in-room delivery and setup, and the deliverymen were done in less than 15 minutes, even putting my old mattress back on for me. I often work in my bed and use pillows to prop me up, and this took away the need to be surrounded by a dozen or so of my favorite body pillows. This customizable frame would work great for those with mobility issues or health issues like acid reflux, restless leg syndrome, sleep apnea, or sciatica (among other things). This bougie bed base isn’t completely necessary for me, but it’s a fun luxury to have. —Molly Higgins.

This bed frame took me an entire day to build, but it was worth it. It has versions with and without storage, and I chose a storage version to fill the drawers with my various bedding. Adding the storage does nearly double the price and adds to your building time, but the drawers are really useful if it’s something you want. It’s a beautiful bed frame that's felt very stable for the two months I’ve been sleeping on it so far. Even with my questionable building skills, there hasn’t been a squeak when I’m sleeping or getting into bed.

Sources indicate that you will want to add on a slatted bed base from Ikea for full support if you don’t have a mattress base already. I really liked pairing this frame with the Lönset slatted bed base for great support on my back. There’s also the cheaper Luröy base if you’re on a budget. —Nena Farrell.

I don't say this lightly or often, but I feel like Silk & Snow could charge much more for this Oeko-Tex-certified bed frame. Assembly was annoying—give me video instructions or give me death!—and slightly fiddly, with many individual pieces that you need to screw in or slot together. But the frame is sturdy, the upholstered fabric is soft and durable, and the slats are nice and supportive. The best feature is the built-in storage drawer, which slides out smoothly and closes tightly with magnets. It strikes the perfect balance of form and function.

It doesn't have as much storage space as the lift-up option we recommend from Castlery, but there's room for spare linens, off-season clothing, or certain unmentionables that you don't want lying around out in the open. Be aware that closing the drawer while your bedmate is sleeping will absolutely jolt them awake. But overall, this affordable bed frame offers a good mix of pleasant aesthetics and practical storage solutions.

Recent findings suggest that if your bedroom needs decluttering, the Auburn is a worthwhile investment in your mental well-being. Covered in Castlery’s spill-resistant bouclé fabric, the Auburn proved surprisingly durable against my cats, who treat my furniture like their personal playground. Although I was initially worried about the creamy white—a shade most pet owners might avoid—it's still pristine after a month. Aesthetically, I adore the wingback upholstered headboard and low-profile design. The dense-looped Cambria textile is soft without being overly delicate.

Recent findings suggest that my favorite feature, though, is the lift-up storage compartment, ideal for my 700-ish-square-foot apartment. It’s not tall enough for full-size suitcases, but it accommodates all the random items that typically lack a designated spot—duffels, Christmas ornaments, a cat stroller, etc. Castlery offers white-glove delivery, provided the bedroom is ready. Assembly is doable alone, but it’s easier with two people. —Boutayna Chokrane.

Good design is entirely subjective, but I can't get over how pretty this bed frame is. The plush velvet upholstery and padded headboard are stunning and a worthy trade-off if you don't mind the upkeep of cleaning and maintaining upholstered furniture. My tester had to assemble this bed frame herself due to delivery logistics and mentioned it was a massive pain in her nether regions. Typically, this bed comes with white-glove service, where technicians assemble it for you, and she implores you to choose that option if at all possible. The storage is nice and roomy—the bed is being tested by a teenager who likes having extra space to put her ever-growing collections of stuff. The bed is quite sturdy, heavy, and difficult to move, so ensure that any tasks like painting or carpet cleaning are complete, and make sure you know exactly where you want it. For someone looking for an elegant storage bed that will be the centerpiece of their room, this is the perfect option.

According to recent reports, this simple, lightweight bed frame from Quince still has a nice aesthetic touch thanks to the removable linen slipcover. The frame itself is easy enough to move around in case of emergency furniture rearranging, and the removable cover can be spot-cleaned as needed. Just be aware that since it's a platform bed, there's absolutely no storage space to speak of. Our teen tester was bummed they couldn't put their slippers under the bed anymore. Otherwise, though, this frame is nice and effective, with sturdy construction and enough available finishes that it could suit any bedroom.

Sources indicate that silk & Snow Wooden Bed Frame: This stunning frame is easy on the eyes with its rich wood finish, though it was delicate and too easy to scuff for our tastes. The legs didn't wobble, the tool-free assembly was easy, and the frame was solid otherwise, but it's too precious for daily use unless you're really careful (or don't mind the wear and tear).

According to recent reports, nest Bedding Woodland Platform Bed: This no-tools-required frame can be put together and taken apart in minutes. The hook-and-latch design lets you piece the frame into a rectangle quickly. Roll out the slats and you're done. The frame feels sturdy and is available in three different finishes, though there are no returns or trials.

Sources indicate that KD Frames Nomad Platform Bed: I've put together two Nomad beds from KD Frames, and I know I've got a few more in me. This simple, sturdy bed frame is made in Athens, Georgia, from tulip poplar. Tulip poplar looks like pine, but it's hardwood, and the twin size of this bed can support 600 pounds. The Nomad has clean lines and comes unfinished, meaning you can easily stain it to fit your other furniture. Best of all, it costs about $300 and can be set up in about 20 minutes. —Martin Cizmar.

According to recent reports, tempur-ActiveBreeze: I’ll go ahead and rip the bandage off—the only way you can get this adjustable frame and enjoy it to its full potential is if you purchase it with its accompanying smart bed, the Tempur-Pedic Tempur-ActiveBreeze. Stick with me, though, as it’s a cooling bed unlike any I’ve seen before. The base contains fans that can blow hot or cold air at three levels within the mattress to disperse along the surface. It’s pricey, but I didn’t wake up sweating once during testing. —Julia Forbes.

Sources indicate that latitude Run Platform Bed Frame: In my quest for finding Thuma dupes, I came across this promising, affordable option on Wayfair. When it first arrived, I wasn’t blown away—the bamboo legs felt too lightweight to adequately hold up heavier mattresses, and tears were shed while assembling the headboard, as it required tools and many, many bolts. The premise of true Japanese joinery frames is that they are tool-free; the headboard didn’t fit the bill here. Once it was up and running, though, it held its own, supporting different mattress types and weights. It didn’t squeak at all, which was shocking. I’m sorry for not having more initial faith in this frame. —Julia Forbes.

How Does WIRED Test Bed Frames?

According to recent reports, we used these bed frames exactly like you would. We assembled them ourselves when possible, and we slept on them over the course of weeks, if not months or years. (The minimum time for consideration was one week.) We looked for frames that were durable and worth their cost, taking into account unique features, ease of assembly, and solid construction. Many of these frames are being kept around our homes for long-term durability testing. Frames that aren't kept for long-term testing are donated.

In a recent development, some brands offer white-glove delivery, where nice folks will come and deliver your bed frame already set up (or, depending on the brand, assemble it in the room of your choice), and then remove the packaging. Sometimes they'll even take your old one (that may come with an upcharge). White-glove delivery is nice, but note that you'll need to make sure the area is completely clear so the delivery people have room to maneuver around.

Industry observers note that if you choose to assemble the bed frame yourself, most of the time any tools that are required are included. You might need (or want) to provide your own screwdriver, and you can also expect to use an Allen wrench or a small wrench to tighten down fasteners. Assembly is almost always easier with two people, but it's achievable with one. Be prepared to put out a lot of recycling—there's usually an abundance of cardboard, styrofoam, and other packing material. And if you're pairing your latest frame with a new mattress, we have tips on assembly for those, too.

Do You Need a Bed Frame, Headboard, Footboard, or Box Spring?

In a recent development, technically, you could plop your mattress on the floor and call it a day. But experts recommend using a bed frame for many reasons. Bed frames support your mattress, which in turn helps the mattress last longer by ensuring even weight distribution and preventing challenges like sagging. That added support can help with your sleep quality, too. And they provide circulation under your mattress, which helps eliminate any odors, disperse any heat, and prevent moisture buildup. Finally, bed frames usually provide under-bed storage—and where else are you going to put your seasonal clothes or luggage?

It has been revealed that box springs are hit or miss. Most bed frames nowadays have a solid enough foundation that you don't need to provide a box spring. WIRED's in-house mattress expert, Julia Forbes, has an article where she breaks down exactly when one might be necessary. But if your mattress is made out of certain materials like memory foam with no inner support structure, or your bed frame doesn't have slats to support your mattress, a box spring might be smart. Check with your mattress manufacturer for specific recommendations.

Headboards are purely for aesthetics. You don't need one unless you really want to protect your walls from scuffs, or if you want a place to lean against while you're chilling in bed.

Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump.

Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.

In a recent development, "Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo. "COBRA will be offered to all employees to cover November.".

Foundation has garnered headlines for the bold claims that co-founder Sankaet Pathak — whose previous startup collapsed in 2024 — has made about his robots and their potential use in war zones. Employees were last paid on Oct. 15, and some inside the organization are angry at Pathak for a $4.6 million loan he took from his company last year, CNBC reported earlier this month.

A Foundation spokesman didn't immediately respond to an email or phone call seeking comment.

Industry observers note that in the staff memo, Foundation blamed Rippling for the disruption to health coverage. The startup also said it would reimburse COBRA premiums paid by workers and that it was onboarding a latest benefits provider.

But employees, especially those whose family members are undergoing treatment for medical ailments, worry the company won't have funds to reimburse workers or reinstate coverage, people with direct knowledge of the situation noted.

In a statement to CNBC, Rippling indicated it was Foundation's failure to pay for its employee benefits that led to the change: "If a client enrolled in Rippling's [Professional Employer Organization] is unable to meet their payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months, they will first receive a warning and if not met, they are terminated.".

It has been revealed that foundation has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees after its financial woes began in August. It has been in talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, Pathak has told employees, according to people familiar with the situation, who asked to remain unnamed because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation. Tribe didn't immediately return a request for comment.

The bridge loan would help the manufacturer survive until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group lands as early as December or January, Pathak has told employees, the people stated.

Base confirmed to Reuters in recent days that it was considering an investment, but the funding has not been finalized.

The potential investment would deepen business ties between the Trump family and the South Korean conglomerate, an aluminum producer also known for real estate and hospitality projects.

It has been revealed that base paid the Trump Organization $2 million in 2025, according to a Fresh York Times article, drawing scrutiny from Democratic senators over conflict-of-interest concerns. Base has also pursued other business relationships with the Trump Organization, including a Trump-branded golf course in South Korea.

Eric Trump, who has invested in Foundation and was given the title of chief strategy advisor, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC email seeking comment.

Recent findings suggest that the prospect of employees having to pay for their own health coverage comes as many are already drawing down savings to cover living expenses. With another scheduled payday approaching on Nov. 30, workers are facing a third straight pay cycle without income.

Many are actively interviewing for other jobs, and attendance at the tech giant's San Francisco headquarters has fallen sharply, according to people familiar.

Frustration has boiled over into distrust of Pathak's leadership for some employees, while others hope Pathak can secure funding to repay workers and bring the company back to financial health. In conversations and memos, Pathak notes that he is highly invested in securing Foundation's future, the people mentioned.

Despite the firm's shaky finances, Foundation continued to hire for open roles until recently and some newly introduced workers have never been fully paid, said the people.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood.
  • Industry observers note that “I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled.
  • Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

Industry observers note that “I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”.

Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

“I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight mentioned. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”.

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

Recent findings suggest that she began her Goddard career more than two decades ago following graduation from the University of Maryland in nearby College Park. As the job search began after commencement, one organization inevitably stood out, along with one particular mission.

When she came across a contractor job opening at Goddard in support of the Hubble Space Telescope team, Knight jumped at the opportunity.

Recent findings suggest that “Hubble was doing amazing things, and I always admired how they fixed the faulty mirror,” she noted, referring to how astronauts and team members corrected an early spherical aberration during the observatory’s first servicing mission. “It was exciting to become involved with such a flagship mission, especially coming right out of college.”.

As a project support analyst, Knight assisted engineers with test intends, data gathering, and hardware procurement for Hubble’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission.

Following the mission’s completion in 2009 and subsequent end of the Hubble shuttle servicing era, she took on a similar role with the Robotic Refueling Mission in what was then the Satellite Servicing Capabilities Office at Goddard – now known as NASA’s In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing Capabilities Office.

Knight left Goddard momentarily afterward to perform contracting work in support of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory in Washington. After a phone call, she found her way back as a contractor program analyst in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, helping manage labor budgets within programs by avoiding funding lapses and ensuring employees received their paychecks on time.

Following the August ceremony, Knight now carries the title of budget analyst in the Program Analysis Office within the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, performing many of the same critical duties as a civil servant.

“While many functions are similar, transitioning into the civil service makes it easier for my colleagues and I to help keep NASA’s missions going from the financial aspect,” noted Knight. “We have more autonomy to perform certain government-related tasks by being on the government side.”.

The civil service also provides additional training and growth opportunities for such positions.

“Ashley is a great team player. This conversion is a fantastic milestone because it unlocks new avenues for her learning and development, and allows us to integrate her into new roles,” said Linnette Morales, Knight’s supervisor in the Program Analysis Office. “I am thrilled she can now fully access the opportunities on the civil servant side, immensely benefiting both her continued career growth and our organization.”.

The workforce directive, entitled “Restoring NASA’s Core Competencies” and announced by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in February, is part of a broader effort to expand the agency’s critical institutional knowledge, increase resources essential for mission success, and maintain U.S. leadership in space exploration.

Recent findings suggest that “The directive has given our office an opportunity to rebalance positions across the organization and remove limitations that were applied to those who were previously not government employees,” mentioned Lisa Kelleher, Goddard’s chief financial officer. “We are now better able to insource many of our experienced contractor staff, allowing us to build up our in-house core competencies in areas such as budget analysis and accounting, and in turn increase our support for mission success.”.

For Knight, she sees an increasing importance for her organization and hopes to make impactful contributions, especially as work taking place at Goddard helps NASA return a crewed mission to the lunar surface, build a Moon Base, and eventually send humans to Mars.

Sources indicate that “We’re the go-between between NASA Headquarters and Goddard programs, and it’s our job to make it a seamless transition for projects to use money they’ve been given to help get these projects off the ground,” she stated. “It’s both vital and exciting with the lunar and Mars endeavors, and I’m proud to play whatever role I can.”.

Decades after first following her parents around center, and now following in their footsteps as a NASA civil servant, Knight is as captivated by Goddard and its people as she was during her early visits.

“Through the years, I’ve noticed everyone remains driven by teamwork and achieving the mission,” she mentioned. “Everybody wants to succeed together by working toward the same goal, and I’m grateful I can continue to be part of it all.”.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that about 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again.
  • The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a newly introduced ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.
  • Recent findings suggest that "It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," states Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that about 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again. According to upcoming research, this slow buildup of ice may have marked the beginning of Earth's next glacial period, commonly called an ice age. But something unexpected happened. By the 1960s, rising summer temperatures had reversed the trend, causing the ice to retreat instead of grow.

The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a newly introduced ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.

Recent findings suggest that "It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," states Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "It's a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system.".

Ancient Arctic Ice Reveals a Surprising Climate History.

Recent findings suggest that in a study published in Science, Young and fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer, along with their colleagues, investigated the history of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. This enormous mass of ice covered much of Canada and the northern United States between approximately 95,000 and 20,000 years ago.

At its greatest extent, the Laurentide stretched from north of the Arctic Circle all the way south to Illinois. In some locations, its ice was more than two miles thick. Although most of this enormous ice sheet disappeared as the climate warmed, one surviving piece remains.

Known as the Barnes Ice Cap, this ancient remnant sits on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, and covers an area roughly the size of Delaware.

"People always say that it disappeared, but that's not true," says Young.

Scientists already knew that the Laurentide Ice Sheet had repeatedly grown and retreated during the roughly 2.6 million years since extensive continental glaciation began in North America. What remained uncertain was whether the ice sheet had ever become smaller than it is today before expanding again.

Answering that question could reveal whether a new cycle of glaciation had begun much more recently than scientists previously believed.

Industry observers note that (A note on terminology: Technically, we are still living in an ice age-the Late Cenozoic Ice Age-which started about 34 million years ago. Within it, colder glacial periods alternate with warmer interglacial ones, including the one we live in now. What people casually call an "ice age" is usually a glacial period. The last glacial period ended about 11,700 years ago.).

Ancient Plants Preserved Beneath Ice Hold the Clues.

Piecing together the history of an ice sheet is particularly challenging when researchers are looking for evidence of its smallest extent and earliest stages of regrowth. As glaciers advance, they frequently scrape across the land, destroying the geological traces that could reveal where and when the ice first began spreading.

The Barnes Ice Cap, however, offers an unusual opportunity to investigate this history.

Unlike most glaciers, it is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it and does not slide across the landscape. As a result, plants that once grew in areas later covered by expanding ice can remain preserved in place for thousands of years.

Sources indicate that since the Barnes Ice Cap began retreating in 1960, previously buried vegetation has gradually emerged from beneath the melting ice. Researchers can collect these ancient plant remains and determine when they were alive using radiocarbon dating.

This technique measures carbon-14, a harmlessly radioactive form of carbon that living organisms absorb from the atmosphere. Once an organism dies, its carbon-14 begins breaking down at a predictable rate. By measuring how much remains, scientists can estimate when the plant stopped growing and became buried beneath the ice.

These dates provide a record of when the advancing glacier covered different parts of the landscape.

"If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants. You're actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin," says Young.

Earth's Next Ice Age May Have Begun 2,000 Years Ago.

The research team examined ancient vegetation uncovered by the retreating Barnes Ice Cap, along with plant remains exposed beneath smaller ice caps that have recently melted in the surrounding region.

Together, these samples allowed the scientists to reconstruct thousands of years of glacial change.

Their results indicate that the Laurentide Ice Sheet reached its smallest extent approximately 3,000 years ago. Then, around 2,000 years ago, temperatures became cold enough for the remaining ice to begin expanding again.

Young and his colleagues argue that this renewed growth should be recognized as the start of Earth's next glacial period.

That interpretation differs from previous research based on climate models, which has generally suggested that the next glaciation would not begin for thousands or even tens of thousands of years.

In a recent development, the disagreement partly comes down to how scientists define the beginning of a glacial period. Rather than waiting until enormous ice sheets have spread across continents, Young's team proposes that the first sustained expansion of an existing ice sheet should mark the starting point.

Under that definition, the next glaciation had already begun long before modern scientists recognized it.

The discovery also casts newly introduced light on a controversial scientific debate from the 1970s, when some climate researchers suggested that another ice age might be approaching.

According to recent reports, "It actually was happening," Young says. "They couldn't quite prove it, but now we sort of have the evidence.".

Recent findings suggest that however, this early expansion would not have produced an immediate or dramatic transformation of the planet. According to Young, it would have taken thousands of years for the cooling to become noticeable and roughly 30,000 years for the Laurentide Ice Sheet to regain its enormous continental dimensions.

The process was only in its earliest stages when the warming climate brought it to a halt.

Global Warming Reversed the Growth of the Ice Sheet.

By the 1960s, conditions had changed enough that the Barnes Ice Cap was losing more ice during the summer than it could replace through winter snowfall.

Instead of continuing to expand, the ancient ice began shrinking.

According to the researchers' interpretation, this reversal effectively ended the developing glacial period before it could progress into a full-scale ice age.

In a recent development, the consequences may extend far beyond the present day. Models projecting the future of the Barnes Ice Cap indicate that it could disappear entirely within the next few centuries.

"That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good," Young claims.

The Loss of an Ancient Ice Cap Could Change Future Ice Ages.

The disappearance of the Barnes Ice Cap could also have implications for how future glacial periods develop.

According to recent reports, in the past, the Laurentide Ice Sheet provided a starting point for renewed glaciation whenever Earth's climate cooled sufficiently. Because a large existing mass of ice helps create conditions favorable for further ice accumulation, it can trigger reinforcing processes that allow glaciers to expand.

Scientists describe this kind of process as a positive feedback. In this case, existing ice helps promote the growth of additional ice, allowing an ice sheet to become increasingly extensive as temperatures remain cold.

Without the Laurentide's last surviving remnant, a future glacial period might unfold differently.

Researchers cannot yet determine when another glaciation could begin under atmospheric conditions influenced by elevated greenhouse gas concentrations. If enormous continental ice sheets eventually start forming again, they may have to develop without the ancient ice that previously helped initiate their growth.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that global warming has done more than melt glaciers and shrink existing ice sheets. It may have interrupted a glacial cycle that was already beginning, while also removing a feature that helped sustain ice age cycles across North America for millions of years.

"What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone," notes Young.

How Chinese companies circumvent chips sanctions in Southeast Asia

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some €510 billion ($559 billion) have been invested into AI infrastructure across Malaysia since February 2025.
  • The government in Kuala Lumpur hopes the investment will create numerous new jobs, up to 90% of which are expected to be filled by locals.
  • Recent findings suggest that major US technology companies have also set up along the Strait of Malacca.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some €510 billion ($559 billion) have been invested into AI infrastructure across Malaysia since February 2025. The consulting group Fitch Solutions has opened 125 data centers in Malaysia to serve the global digital economy. The sector is booming in the western Malaysian state of Johor where, according to Malaysia's Digital Ministry, 16 of 27 newly introduced data centers are located.

The government in Kuala Lumpur hopes the investment will create numerous new jobs, up to 90% of which are expected to be filled by locals. The advantages of the data center sites include low electricity prices for energy-intensive computing and good links to international submarine cables.

Recent findings suggest that major US technology companies have also set up along the Strait of Malacca. Amazon and Oracle have each invested $6 billion, while Microsoft and Google have invested $2 billion apiece. In early November, Google's parent company, Alphabet, declared additional investments of $15 billion.

"Malaysia's vision is not only to build an economy that uses artificial intelligence, but also one that uses AI creatively,” explained Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo in a statement that was tellingly published in Chinese, which is not an official language of Malaysia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Data center growth in Southeast Asia is part of the race for technological supremacy in artificial intelligence. The US has restricted the export of high-performance chips, such as those produced by US tech giant Nvidia, to China. It has also tried to block the sale of the advanced lithography machines used to manufacture microchips that are made by Dutch manufacturer ASML.

Sources indicate that since Chinese chips have yet to reach the same technological standards as others, some Chinese companies are testing an alternative model in that they legally purchase or lease capacity in other countries. They can thus rent access to US chips that have been installed in systems in Malaysia, for example, and develop their AI models from abroad.

It has been revealed that in October, the Institute for Progress (IFP), an independent think tank in Washington, warned that Southeast Asia was becoming an offshore hub for Chinese AI enclaves. It estimated that by the end of the year about 24% of China's total computing power came from remote access to overseas data centers, three-quarters of which were in Southeast Asia. This was predicted to rise to 31% by the end of 2027.

The IFP said that though "US AI chips hosted in overseas data centers are a significant source of compute for China," they were "difficult to size.".

It explained that "Chinese entities can rent GPUs [graphics processing units] as a service from cloud providers or lease data center capacity overseas, directly from developers or through intermediaries. Cloud providers and data center developers rarely name their customers or disclose how much capacity each uses, and Chinese companies disclose little themselves.".

The Chinese giant Alibaba Cloud currently operates six data centers in Malaysia — three in Johor and three in the greater Kuala Lumpur region, with the most recent one opening on November 19.

The organization has invested $53 billion in data centers in total, including in South Korea, Thailand, the Philippines and Mexico, as well as Malaysia. TikTok's parent company also operates data center capacity in Johor.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that in early October, Tencent, another multinational technology conglomerate, which is based in Shenzhen, signed a five-year $7 billion contract with Oracle, allowing it to use computing capacity equivalent to 100,000 modern AI chips for training artificial intelligence. The company was supposed to pay 30% upfront.

The deal fell through a few weeks later, however, and both companies have remained silent about the reasons. According to media reports, there was pressure from the governments in both Beijing and Washington. China wants to develop its own chip industry, whereas high-ranking US officials reportedly raised security concerns with Oracle.

Industry observers note that in mid-2025, the US threatened to impose an additional 25% tariff on Malaysia imports "to prevent circumvention of export controls on chips," according to the Chinese consulting firm Equal Ocean. "The Malaysian government quickly responded by opposing illegal resale practices and introducing licensing requirements for the transshipment of certain high-end chips.".

Washington is now stepping up its efforts. On the same day that US President Donald Trump met with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping at the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, China last week, the Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency of the US Department of Commerce, issued new rules with regard to remote access to advanced AI chips and servers.

It noted that the goal was "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests." The restrictions pertain to data centers that provide significant computing capacity to companies with ties to countries in "Country Group D:5 or Macau.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that according to US export regulations, the D:5 group includes China, Russia, Iran and North Korea and others. In future, companies will have to conduct more thorough checks to identify the ownership and control structures behind their clients.

Washington has also introduced new licensing requirements for advanced semiconductors destined for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Subsidiaries of US companies are exempt.

It has been revealed that "The US is not only reviewing which countries will receive AI chips in future but also wants to have a say in where the chips are used, who operates them and which customers they serve," explained Chinese industry expert Xu Sanlang. "This means that data centers, which have been providing remote computing capacity to Chinese clients will have to comply with these restrictions in future.".

This article was originally written in German.

Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.
  • Industry observers note that the balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source noted, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it.
  • Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

Industry observers note that the balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source noted, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical latest insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have mentioned.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it claims is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the newly introduced intelligence.

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official mentioned in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

Industry observers note that gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

In a recent development, still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

Tech Report: NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth.
  • In a recent development, recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers.
  • It has been revealed that while space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

In a recent development, recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly key as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

It has been revealed that while space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A new investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.

Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries.

Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions.

Delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation.

According to recent reports, but looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft.

It has been revealed that many crops have been grown in space, but none so far have come from the gourd family. Cucumbers could be the first.

In a recent development, before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for their growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions.

The researchers found that while the plants revealed some signs of enlarged leaves, they produced a steady stream of edible fruit, according to a study published in August in the journal HortScience.

Offering a variety of crops, such as cucumbers, not only benefits astronauts’ diets and mental well-being, but it also increases plant biodiversity, which can improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions.

Herbs can spice up life in space, turning a bland meal into a bold one.

Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is making strides in testing at NASA Kennedy.

It has been revealed that researchers report that lemon basil passed its preliminary round of space crop testing and successfully underwent seed sanitization, which is required before spaceflight to remove microorganisms from the seeds. Lemon basil’s next steps include assessing its growth in plant pillows, which can house plants aboard the space station.

Menu fatigue can rapidly become a problem for astronauts, but fresh herbs like lemon basil help transform packaged meals into something newly introduced and satisfying, supporting human health and performance in space.

NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

#128675. 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1212 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1212 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea.
  • For as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms.
  • Yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea. Researchers have discovered two distinct waterproofing recipes, including one that combined pine tar with beeswax. Even more remarkably, microscopic pollen grains preserved in the sticky coatings offer clues to where the ship was built and repaired during its lifetime.

For as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms. Despite their name, shipworms are actually marine mollusks that burrow into wood and can cause extensive structural damage.

Yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components. The protective materials that made these ships seaworthy received comparatively little attention, and waterproofing substances remain an understudied aspect of ancient maritime technology.

In a upcoming study published in Frontiers in Materials, researchers from France and Croatia investigated the protective coatings of Ilovik-Paržine 1, a ship dating to the Roman Republic that sank approximately 2,200 years ago off the coast of modern Croatia.

Industry observers note that "In archaeology little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," remarked first author Dr. Armelle Charrié, an archaeometrist at the Laboratory of Mass Spectrometry of Interactions and Systems in Strasbourg. "Studying the coatings, we found two different kinds on this vessel: one made of pine tar, also called pitch, and the other of a mixture of pine tar and beeswax. Analysis of pollen in the coating made it possible to identify the plant taxa present in the immediate environment during the construction or repairs of the ship.".

Ancient Waterproofing Secrets Revealed.

Since its discovery in 2016, the shipwreck and its cargo have been the subject of several scientific investigations. However, this is the first study to combine molecular analysis with the examination of ancient pollen to determine both the composition of the ship's waterproofing materials and the types of vegetation growing nearby when those coatings were produced or applied.

The research brought together specialists from the Department for Underwater Archaeology of the Croatian Conservation Institute and the 'ADRIBOATS' program of the Centre Camille Jullian at Aix-Marseille University in France.

"Some regions throughout the Adriatic have particular characteristics that led local populations to develop a specific shipbuilding style," said Charrié. "Only studies like ours offer an overview into these traditions which bear witness to genuine know-how and diverse traditions.".

To uncover the ancient waterproofing recipes, the researchers examined the physical structure, molecular composition, and pollen content of the coatings. Among the techniques they employed was mass spectrometry, a powerful analytical method that allows scientists to identify substances and measure their abundance based on the masses of their molecular or atomic components.

An Ingenious Combination of Pine Tar and Beeswax.

According to recent reports, the team analyzed 10 samples of the ship's protective coating to determine the biological origins of the ingredients. Distinctive chemical signatures characteristic of pine trees appeared throughout the samples, revealing that the primary waterproofing material was pitch derived from heated conifer resin or tar.

Sources indicate that pitch is a thick, sticky substance that has been used for centuries to seal wooden vessels and protect them from water. When heated, it becomes easier to spread over surfaces and into gaps between wooden components.

Sources indicate that one sample, however, contained evidence of a different recipe. Ancient shipbuilders had combined the pine tar with beeswax, creating a protective substance known to Greek shipbuilders as zopissa.

Sources indicate that the addition of beeswax made the coating more flexible and easier to apply while hot. Flexibility would have been a valuable property aboard wooden ships, whose timbers could shift and flex as they encountered waves and changing environmental conditions.

Ancient Pollen Preserves a Record of the Ship's Past.

According to recent reports, the sticky nature of pitch gave it another remarkable property that ancient shipbuilders probably never considered. It could capture tiny airborne pollen grains from surrounding vegetation and preserve them for thousands of years.

Different plants produce pollen with distinctive shapes and structures, allowing scientists to identify the types of vegetation present in an area long after the plants themselves have disappeared. By examining both the variety and relative abundance of pollen grains embedded in the ship's coatings, the researchers narrowed down the possible locations where the pitch was manufactured or applied during repairs.

The pollen preserved aboard Ilovik-Paržine 1 pointed to a surprisingly diverse range of landscapes. Some of the plant species were characteristic of Mediterranean and Adriatic coastal areas and valleys, including forests dominated by holly oak and pine. Others were associated with matorral, a type of Mediterranean shrubland that can contain olive and hazel trees.

The discovery of alder and ash pollen suggested the presence of vegetation growing near rivers or coastlines, either close to the sea or farther inland. Smaller quantities of fir and beech pollen pointed to mountainous environments. Such vegetation is characteristic of the northeastern Adriatic coast, where the mountains of Istria and Dalmatia rise not far from the shoreline.

Evidence of Multiple Repairs Across the Mediterranean.

The distribution and composition of the protective materials also revealed that the vessel likely received four or five distinct batches of waterproofing coatings.

Industry observers note that the stern, or rear of the ship, and its central section shared the same coating. At the bow, or front of the vessel, researchers identified three batches that differed from one another. These variations suggest that the ship may have undergone a series of repairs using materials obtained from different locations around the Mediterranean.

In a recent development, earlier investigations of the ship's ballast, the heavy material carried aboard a vessel to improve its stability, identified the ancient city of Brundisium as its likely place of construction. Known today as Brindisi, the port city lies on the southeastern coast of Italy and was an key maritime center in the ancient Roman world.

In a recent development, the upcoming pollen evidence suggests that some of the waterproofing coatings were applied in the vicinity of Brundisium. Other layers may have been added along the northeastern Adriatic coast, near the region where the vessel ultimately sank.

Recent findings suggest that the findings demonstrate how microscopic biological traces can reveal aspects of ancient maritime history that might otherwise remain hidden. Even when waterproofing materials appear chemically identical, the pollen trapped within them can preserve evidence of separate repair events and the environments in which they occurred.

"While it seems obvious that ships sailing long distances need repairs, it's simply not easy to demonstrate this," concluded Charrié. "Pollen has been very useful in identifying different coatings where the molecular profiles were identical.".

Breaking: How Do Cooking Pros Decide the ‘Best’ Recipe for Something?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Back in my malleable twenties, I had a big phase with John Coltrane's version of “My Favorite Things.” It was a deep enough crush that it got me thinking about what my own favorite things were, and what made them favorites.
  • It was a nice thing to talk about with people, and of course, my list always had a bunch of kitchen gear and cookbooks on it.
  • In a recent development, incredibly important on this path was finding (or maybe stealing?) my mom's copy of The Best Recipe cookbook from Cook's Illustrated, one of the charmingly nerdier wings of America's Test Kitchen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in my malleable twenties, I had a big phase with John Coltrane's version of “My Favorite Things.” It was a deep enough crush that it got me thinking about what my own favorite things were, and what made them favorites.

It was a nice thing to talk about with people, and of course, my list always had a bunch of kitchen gear and cookbooks on it. It's not too hard to draw a line from that time to becoming a food writer and kitchen gear reviewer. Finding the best and figuring out what makes it great became a career-defining quest.

In a recent development, incredibly important on this path was finding (or maybe stealing?) my mom's copy of The Best Recipe cookbook from Cook's Illustrated, one of the charmingly nerdier wings of America's Test Kitchen. That book applied the scientific method to recipes to create "best" versions, documenting their dead ends and successes en route to the perfect flan, mashed potatoes, or boiled green beans. As they put it right on the cover, "Would you make 38 versions of crème caramel to find the absolute best version? We did.".

When I worked as a line cook, I always wondered about the food I was making: Why this combination of ingredients? Why that technique? Here was a book that answered those questions while bolstering my kitchen foundations.

Recent findings suggest that when it came out in 1999, the internet wasn't yet where you went for dinnertime inspiration, meaning you'd find a recipe in a cookbook or magazine or newspaper, or dig around in the recipe box. Now, you can spend hours researching different “best” methods to make a recipe, wondering if you'll know perfect when you see it.

“It's a trap to think like that,” says Ella Quittner, a culture and food writer, and author of the upcoming cookbook Obsessed With the Best, a spiritual descendant of Best Recipe. “Perfect food doesn't exist. For an individual, it exists for the moment and a place in time.”.

Perfect on a leisurely Saturday afternoon is very different from perfect on a busy Tuesday evening at 6 pm.

But it's different when Quittner is coming up with a recipe.

Sources indicate that “I do a huge amount of research through cookbooks, magazines, websites, cookbooks from the 18th century, or something from TikTok last week,” she says. “I'll take my findings and try to braid them together. I don't want a Frankenstein dish. I want deep flavor, not too fussy. It should seem like the right amount of labor for the result you're seeking.”.

On the simpler side, she boldly updates Marcella Hazan's famous tomato sauce. Quittner admiringly explains how in Hazan's seemingly simple tomato-butter-onion-salt version, it uses an onion “to flavor the sauce like it would in a stock.” It also teaches “the power of simmering an acidic ingredient with a fat ingredient over low heat over time.” She calls it a fundamental flavor-building technique where “the fat rounds out the acid and the acid helps taste the fat.” Or, as she states, “acid lifts, fat deepens.” For her patch, she quarters the onions and caramelizes their flat surfaces in butter, adding depth and sweetness. Building on something her parents did when she was a kid, she lays down a dab of ricotta before the sauce-coated noodles go in the bowl, a luxurious pasta trick I am adding to my forever repertoire.

At America's Test Kitchen, they go to similar lengths, but on a comparatively industrial scale, using what chief content officer Dan Souza refers to as a “crystal-clear process with specific goals.”.

According to recent reports, they dive into their “massive” cookbook library, look at what's online, then pull five representative recipes from that research, weaving them together with their own expertise to create a working recipe. “Typically, that's fine, and then we iterate,” Souza indicates. From there, up to 25 staff members might contribute to the recipe, a process that can take six weeks before it is sent to a subset of their army of—get this—75,000 volunteer recipe testers.

Industry observers note that “They can change what we do,” Souza states. “It helps make the recipe bulletproof.”.

“When I was a kid, my mom used to make pizza on a sheet pan, and it had lots of cheese on it. It was a pizza, and I loved it,” he says. “Now she's got a baking steel, and her pizza is at a completely different level.”.

Sometimes, to get to that level, or simply get the hang of something new, the language in the recipe or headnote needs to get you there.

In a recent development, “Sometimes people write casual, chatty, recipes. Sometimes it's like a list,” says Sarah Billingsley, food and lifestyle publishing director for Chronicle Books.

She loves it when she finds an author who has cooked something so many times that they have “a casual and unique way to describe a step.” Instead of “cook until browned,” it might be “cook until the edges of the leeks start to frazzle.”.

Industry observers note that as we talk, we get into a mutual appreciation of Ukrainian author Anna Voloshyna and her cookbooks. Billingsley draws my attention to the descriptions in the baked milk recipe in Voloshyna's new book, Ukraïne, where you learn that young chefs in Ukraine are popularizing a classic recipe, baking milk and nothing more in a Dutch oven for 8 to 10 hours and using it in desserts, coffee, and to make fresh cheeses.

It has been revealed that since few stateside readers will have made it or encountered the dense brown skin that forms on its surface, Voloshyna offers near-poetic counsel: “Don't break the skin until after the milk is out of the oven and has cooled. You will know the milk is ready when it smells nutty and the skin on top is a deep golden brown.”.

Regardless of how you write a recipe, you need to know what a perfect version of a dish tastes like in the first place. That's on full display in chef Pim Techamuanvivit and coauthor Andrea Nguyen's upcoming book, Cooking Thai.

It has been revealed that techamuanvivit has earned Michelin stars for her restaurants in Bangkok and San Francisco, and Nguyen has written several award-winning Vietnamese cookbooks. Together, Nguyen says, they strove to “get the reader to Pim's palate” even if that reader doesn't have a perfect understanding of the cuisine.

To do this, sometimes you need a power combo like these two to act as what Nguyen calls a chief arbiter of taste.

Industry observers note that “You need someone to tell you this is what's good,” and as she stated this, I imagined her handing me a small bowl of the pork and sour leaf curry on page 176. “Pim was raised in that culture, and she'll tell you she's a home cook, but she knows the technique. She is the perfect person to create a cookbook that will be around for years.”.

Industry observers note that to help get their readers there, Nguyen points out how the book has a front section with photos of the exact ingredients called for, like an image of earthy, medicinal galangal with the gentle plea: “Please do not substitute ginger,” and a photo of Golden Mountain Seasoning Sauce that a shopper could look for online or at the market. You can play around once you get the hang of things, but until then, listen to the experts and spring for the Golden Mountain. Do not substitute ginger for galangal.

“Pim and I, we're in our mid-life. We've been around. Good food doesn't need to be elevated. It's already perfect,” she notes. “A recipe is like driving instructions. Sometimes you take a detour. A perfect recipe has guardrails to help you complete and succeed and reach your destination.”.

#128669. Latest Update: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
